catalog_quote: Stress in Nungon is not contrastive. That is, there is only one minimal pair in the extant corpus that possibly exemplifies an instance in which stress could distinguish between two otherwise-identical words ... Stress seems to be related to both quantity and quality: closed syllables, long vowels, and diphthongs attract stress, as does, to a lesser extent, the vowel /u/ ... Stress in nouns, adjectives and adverbs follows a different system than stress in verbs. | Two-syllable words with open second syllables are almost always stressed on the first syllable. | Two-syllable words with closed second syllables vary in stress assignment. Most two-syllable words with a closed second syllable and an open first syllable have stress on the second syllable, but there are quite a few exceptions ... | Three-syllable single-morpheme words are usually stressed on the first syllable (the antepenult). ... Exceptions with penultimate stress do exist, however ... | Four- and five-syllable monomorphemic words are rare in Nungon. Among the longer monomorphemic words that do exist, stress is unpredictable. | Final verbs are usually stressed on the first syllable of the word, unless inflectional suffixation creates diphthongs in other syllables—then these diphthongs tend to be stressed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per phonological word; stress is non-contrastive (one doubtful minimal pair). Default is initial stress: disyllables with an open second syllable, trisyllabic monomorphemes, and inflected final verbs are normally stressed on the first syllable. Heavy syllables (closed syllables, long vowels, diphthongs) attract stress, and /u/ weakly does so: most disyllables of shape (C)V.CVC are stressed on the closed final syllable (with many lexical exceptions, Table 2.8 p. 100), and suffixes that create diphthongs in verbs draw stress onto the diphthong. Four- and five-syllable monomorphemes have unpredictable stress. Stress assignment is described as predictable in verbs and 'not entirely predictable' in nouns (p. 66). Singular pertensive suffixes -na/-a/-no and adjectivizers -no/-ni shift stress rightward onto the syllable immediately before the suffix (obu 'hand' [ˈɔ.bu] -> obu-na [ɔˈbu.na]), except in CaCa(C) words; suffixes themselves are never stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned: Near Future forms carry secondary stress on the first element of the historical auxiliary (dawi-wang-ka-t [ˈda.βi.waŋˌkhat˺], p. 106); in past Habitual constructions the inflected auxiliary it- 'be' bears only secondary stress within the phonological word (p. 107); secondary-stress marks also appear in transcriptions of 4-5 syllable words (p. 101) and some suffixed forms (p. 103, 109).
new_statements.exceptions: Five disyllables with open /u/-final second syllable stressed finally (akka, dogu, imu, ittu, muyu, p. 99); many CV.CVC disyllables with initial stress despite closed final syllable (Table 2.8, p. 100); trisyllables with penultimate stress (imöndim, hanggamba, isuna, orongmök, Pahamit, p. 101); 4-5 syllable monomorphemes unpredictable (p. 101); in verbs, monosyllabic vowel-final roots with -nung or -gu-ng take final stress (hi-gu-ng, p. 105); Ø-class 2sg imperatives stress the root-final diphthong (ongo-i [ɔˈŋɔɪ], p. 106); Different Subject suffixes creating diphthongs shift stress (iso-un-a [iˈsɔu.na], p. 109); reduplicated verbal roots stress the second copy, reduplicated non-verbs the first (pp. 110-111); loans (e.g. from Kâte) irregular.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the phonological word is the domain (one primary stressed syllable per phonological word, §2.4.2 p. 84); Dependent verb + auxiliary 'be' can fuse into one phonological word with a single primary stress (§2.7.3); compounds carry one primary stress vs. two under juxtaposition (§2.6.7). Forms are citation/lexicon forms plus inflected verbs; one waveform/spectrogram (Figure 2.2) illustrates a verb form. Sentence intonation is treated separately (§2.9, §13.3). Description is of the Towet dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Sarvasy 2014 describes the Towet village dialect of Nungon, the southern dialect cluster of Yau-Nungon (Glottolog dialect head1238 'Nungon'), with brief comparative notes on Yawan, Worin, Kotet and Sagain dialects (Table 2.7, p. 98). Yau proper (Glottolog nort2910, lower Uruwa valley, the SIL-documented variety behind the ISO name) is not the described variety; the thesis notes Yau and other dialects have a word-final glottal stop that Towet lacks (p. 2).
